The purest implementation of this is Merchants of Amsterdam, which features a spring-load mechanism that gradually reduces the price until someone hits it, winning the bid. This category also includes the mechanism where items slide down a track, with the cost decreasing as it does so. This is a common implementation of Open Drafting such as in Through the Ages: A Story of Civilization. An alternative but logically equivalent process is Increase Value of Unchosen Resources.

name: Auction: Multiple Lot
description: An auction in which players simultaneously bid on Multiple Lots in parallel, instead of bidding for one lot at a time serially. The actual format of the auction can follow any of the auction mechanisms. For example, in Revolution! players perform a simultaneous Sealed Bid Auction on 12 different actions.

name: Auction: Once Around
description: The players each have one opportunity to bid, either passing or raising the prior bidder. The order of bids is determined by one of the Turn Order structures. After the last player has their opportunity to bid, the high bidder wins. Although this helps shorten the auction (as increasing game length is a pitfall of including auctions), it strongly favors the last player to bid, as they know what their winning bid needs to be, so the designer needs to take care to balance properly. Examples include Modern Art and Medici.

name: Auction: English
description: An auctioneer asks for bids of a certain amount and players indicate their willingness to bid at that amount, usually by holding up a hand or paddle, or by calling out. Players are permitted to adjust the increment of the bid, usually by shouting out their actual bid, though this is done infrequently, and usually either to indicate a smaller increment than the auctioneer requests, or a much larger one. When a certain amount of time with no increases occurs, or it is clear that no one wishes to raise the current bid, the auctioneer declares that the high bidder is the winner.

name: Passed Action Token
description: Players possess one or more Action Tokens. Those who have an Action Token may take a turn, then they pass the token clockwise, allowing the next player to perform an action. Actions are performed in real time; - there is no pausing and structure within the turn. Typically, to prevent stalling and to keep the game moving, in games with multiple Action Tokens, if both tokens are held by the same player, then they suffer a penalty. Camelot and Diner are examples.

name: Closed Economy Auction
description: Closed-Economy is a meta-mechanism that can modify any auction type. In a Closed-Economy Auction, all the money spent in the auction is paid out to the auction participants themselves. For example, in Nightmare Productions, the winning bid is distributed evenly between the non-winning players, and losing bids is the only way to gain more money.

name: Auction: Fixed Placement
description: Fixed Placement is a meta-mechanism that modifies a multiple-lot auction by creating rules about which lots players may bid on, and representing bids visually on a board or cards. It is often combined with constrained-value bids. A Fixed-Placement auction ends when every player passes and/or no player has the right to bid further. The highest bidder for each lot wins the lot. Good examples of this mechanism are in Amun-Re and Vegas Showdown. In these games, there is a track below each lot up for auction. Each player places a marker on the lot they are interested in, at the value they want to pay. If another player wants to bid on that lot they do it by placing their bid marker on a space higher than the current bidder. The outbid player retrieves their bid token, and may place it on the same lot at a higher price, or another lot. When all players have placed their token, the bids are resolved.

name: Auction: Dexterity
description: A Dexterity Auction requires performance of some act of dexterity to submit a valid bid. Typically, this would involve the bid marker itself being placed into some valid bidding area, but other methods for implementing this may be used. For example, in Going, Going, GONE!, players place tokens in cups in real time to represent their bid.

name: Auction Compensation
description: Losing bidders in an auction receive a lesser award in place of the lot they bid on.

name: Lane Battler
description: An Area Control or Area Majority mechanism that includes linear of other spatial elements. Lane Battlers arrange the areas the players are fighting over in a line. Each location is called a lane. The origin of the name comes from the Multiplayer Online Battle Arena (MOBA) genre of video games that featured players facing off from opposing bases on opposite sides of a map. Several lanes connect the bases, and heroes and minions would stream down these lanes to do conflict in a kind of tug of war. Tabletop implementations often abstract the movement of troops down each individual lane but retain the notion of adjacency between the lanes.

name: Facing
description: Units have an orientation relative to the board that impacts play. "Units" are not game components like orientable neutral tiles in games like Carcassonne.

name: Auction: Dutch Priority
description: A Dutch Priority Auction is a multiple-lot auction in which prices for the lots are determined based on the number of bids placed on the lots up for bid. The winning bidder is the first player, in bid priority, who chooses to pay the current price for a lot, which is equal to the number of bidding tokens there. Priority may be determined by a variety of factors, including global turn order or turn order for each lot based on order of bid placement. Players may typically pass on the purchase when they are the priority bidder by removing their bidding token. This has the effect of reducing the price for the lot by one. The Speicherstadt introduced this mechanism. In that, players place meeples one at a time on different lots to be bid on. After all meeples are placed, each lot is evaluated. The player with the first meeple placed on a lot may purchase it, but must pay a price equal to the total number of meeples. If they cannot or will not purchase it, they take their meeple back, and the next meeple in line may purchase, now at $1 less. This opens up lots of opportunity for counterplay and brinkmanship in a relatively simple system.

name: Single Play
description: A game intended to be played one time by the same player(s). Single Play games are sometimes referred to as “One Shot” games, because they are intended to be played a single time. Typically, they have puzzles, mysteries, or surprises, so once a player has experienced and “solved” the game, derived cannot be enjoyed the same way again.

name: Expiring Actions
description: This is a meta‑mechanism that modifies other mechanisms. An action is available until some game condition occurs that removes the action from play. Expiring actions are very common in games, and they often feature a trade‑off between keeping an action available and obtaining some other goal, such as scoring points. For example, in Valley of the Kings, a deck‑building game, players add Action cards to their deck, but only score points by entombing these Action cards, removing them permanently from their deck. This “score‑or‑play” dynamic is common to the mechanism. In Kokopelli, players seek to collect several copies of the same Action card to score as a set. Until the set is complete, the card provides a powerful action or benefit—so powerful that sometimes, opponents will choose to complete a player’s set and gift them the associated points, to neutralize the powerful ability offered by the incomplete set.

name: Visual Restriction
description: Game components are hidden from the view of one or more players. A hand of cards is an ancient and ubiquitous method of making information visible to only one player. This mechanism is intended for lesser‑used varieties of visual restriction and their applications beyond the usual methods of keeping items facedown, in hand, or behind a screen.

name: Handicaps
description: The game gives some players an advantage to level skill differences. A handicap system allows players of different skill levels to play a game together while maintaining its competitive balance. Handicap systems are common in social sports activities such as golf and bowling but are only occasionally implemented formally in board games. The ancient game Go is perhaps the oldest example of a formal handicap system.

name: Algorithmic Resolution
description: A multistep resolution process with little to no player interaction. Some resolution systems require the players to go through multiple steps with no player decision points. An early familiar and simple example is the public domain card game War. Players flip cards, and if there is a tie each player plays three cards face down, and then a fourth face up to see who wins all the cards played. If there is another tie, the process is repeated, etc. Players have no choice during this process (although they have no choice the entire game, so it can be argued that the game itself is 100% algorithmic resolution).

name: Retirement
description: Retirement is a game‑end trigger. The game will continue until all players choose to retire from the game, or until all but one player chooses to retire, and that player continues to play until some additional game‑end trigger occurs.
